$comment: The guided design loop's terms (FEAT-018 GDL-79): what each means, and why it is valuable to the person. The agent explains each the first time it comes up; ux-builder-design explain prints them. ids: the short IDs the guide shows, what kind of thing each names and where it lives; the agent names the kind with an ID the first time it shows one.

terms.means: A point where the agent stops and asks you one question, and waits for your answer before going on.
terms.why: The decisions that shape the design are yours, recorded in your words, not made for you along the way.

terms.means: A small file the guide keeps with the app (.ux-builder/design-state.json): where the process is, what is chosen, what is assumed and what you approved.
terms.why: Any session, and any person, can pick up exactly where the last one left off.

terms.means: The app's requirements and design documents (docs/helix/): the product vision, the PRD, features and user stories.
terms.why: The design follows what the product is meant to do, and changes to requirements go through a reviewed proposal, never a silent edit.

terms.means: What the rest of the design is built on: the experience brief, target users, jobs, user stories, business rules and decisions. You review each kind as one table, every row in full.
terms.why: A mistake here spreads into every journey, screen and test, so this is where your careful attention pays most; what is built from the foundations needs only its exceptions checked.

terms.means: One view of what is built from the foundations: each job, the tasks that serve it, their journeys and the screens they walk, with the exceptions (a job nothing serves, a screen on no journey, a new assumption) listed one by one.
terms.why: You check that nothing was missed or added without reading every task and screen again; approving the map approves them.

terms.means: One page saying what the product is, who it is for, the outcome it should give them, the jobs it serves, its principles and constraints, and what is still unknown.
terms.why: Everyone works from the same intent, and every point says whether it is confirmed, assumed or a hypothesis.

terms.means: A short statement of something a user needs to do and why: As a <user> I want <capability> so that <benefit>, with acceptance criteria.
terms.why: It keeps each piece of work tied to a real need, small enough to design, build and test.

terms.means: A testable condition a story must meet, written Given <situation>, when <action>, then <result>, with an ID such as US-002-AC1.
terms.why: It makes "done" checkable: tests cite it, and the test kit uses it as what success looks like.

terms.means: Something taken as true for now without evidence, recorded so it can be checked.
terms.why: Unchecked assumptions are where designs fail; listing them shows what to test first.

terms.means: A proposed idea about users or the design, stated so evidence can confirm or refute it, with how it would be confirmed.
terms.why: It separates what we believe from what we know, so neither you nor the agent mistakes a guess for a fact.

terms.means: A group of people the product is for, described by their situation: their context, needs and the jobs they hold (U-1, U-2). A segment, not an invented person.
terms.why: Designs are judged for someone: the same screen can suit one user and fail another, and tests recruit and report by them.

terms.means: The progress a person is trying to make, in their terms and independent of any product: "find water I'm allowed to fish, near me" (J-1).
terms.why: It keeps the design on the need rather than on features, and every task traces back to a job.

terms.means: A research source (an interview, analytics, support tickets, a survey, a test session), recorded with only the masked quotes the design relies on (EV-1).
terms.why: It is what turns a hypothesis into something confirmed, and it can be pointed to later.

terms.means: How sure the evidence makes us about a user or a job: low, medium or high, rated apart from how important it is.
terms.why: An important job resting on little evidence is a risk worth seeing before designing around it.

terms.means: The plan of the app's screens and how people move through them (app.blueprint.json): its tasks, journeys, screens and actions, written before any screen is built.
terms.why: It can be checked, scored, compared and prototyped before code exists, so problems are cheap to fix.

terms.means: Something a user must accomplish in the product, with its goal, the jobs it serves, its inputs, what the system does, what success looks like and what can go wrong (T-1).
terms.why: It describes the work independently of screens, so the simplest way to do it can be found.

terms.means: A rule of the business the product must follow, defined once in HELIX: "only stretches with public access can be saved" (BR-1).
terms.why: Rules users only meet as errors cause frustration; designing how they learn of a rule and recover from it prevents that.

terms.means: The path a user takes through the screens to complete a task, step by step (J-find).
terms.why: It is what gets compared, scored for effort, prototyped and walked in tests.

terms.means: Another blueprint for the same tasks, such as map first versus list first (app.blueprint.<name>.json).
terms.why: Comparing two or more designs before choosing finds simpler ones and shows what each costs the user.

terms.means: Nine dimensions of UX quality (task effectiveness, efficiency, cognitive load and others), each with a prediction and later what people actually did; never an overall score.
terms.why: It makes a design's strengths and weaknesses visible one by one, and shows where predictions were wrong.

terms.means: A short record of a design question, the alternatives, the choice and why, its assumptions and whether it has been tested (UXD-1).
terms.why: The reason survives: later changes can see why it is the way it is, and whether that still holds.

terms.means: The kind of experience the app gives its users: responsive web (screens from phone to desktop), chat (the conversation is the interface) or hybrid chat (replies include cards and inline screens).
terms.why: It decides which patterns, navigation and rules apply, so it is settled before any screen is drawn.

terms.means: A range of screen widths the app must work at: compact (phones), medium (small tablets), expanded (tablets and small laptops), large and extra-large (desktops).
terms.why: Each size class can need a different layout; naming them up front means every wireframe and prototype is drawn for the screens people will really use.

terms.means: One place in the app, with its purpose, the information it shows in order of priority, and the actions on it.
terms.why: Stating a screen's purpose and priorities first keeps it focused and makes the order of its content deliberate.

terms.means: A ready-made screen layout from the SDK (a list, a record's details, a form, a wizard) that a screen is built from.
terms.why: Known patterns behave consistently and accessibly, so people recognize them and less is built from scratch.

terms.means: A plain drawing of a screen's layout and content, without the final look.
terms.why: It shows structure and priorities quickly, before effort goes into visual detail.

terms.means: A disposable, clickable set of pages generated from a blueprint to answer one design question; never app code.
terms.why: You can try a design in minutes and throw it away, before anything is built.

terms.means: The app's look: its colours, type, shapes and logo, applied through role tokens so every screen follows it. Each released theme pairs a brand with a design system (Material 3, Fluent 2, Carbon, Databricks or its own).
terms.why: Chosen once the design is settled, so the look serves the experience; a theme made from your brand in the theme builder makes the app yours without hand-styling any screen.

terms.means: The chosen design built in the app itself, on a branch, with sample data, ready to show test users.
terms.why: People test something real; it becomes production code only after you say it is validated enough.

terms.means: What you need to test with people: scenarios in the user's words, success criteria, a script, a consent note, a screener and an observation sheet (TK-1).
terms.why: Tests are consistent and fair, and their results connect back to the stories and journeys.

terms.means: A problem seen or predicted, with its evidence, severity and a fix, labelled as a human observation or an agent recommendation (F-…).
terms.why: Each problem is specific enough to act on, and you can tell what people did from what the agent thinks.

terms.means: The results of an evaluation: the method, the tasks, what people did against what was predicted, findings by journey and what was not tested (UER-1).
terms.why: It is the evidence for deciding what to fix and whether the design is ready to build.

terms.means: An automatic check of the running app in every theme and in light and dark: the interaction and AI rules, contrast, and anything that is not the theme's (a hard-coded colour, a stray font). `npm run audit` runs it.
terms.why: It catches broken and off-brand screens in minutes, before anyone spends time testing them.

terms.means: A walk through each journey from your user stories in the running app, inspecting every screen state, applying usability heuristics and measuring each task, ending in a report with proposed changes. The agent runs it with `ux-builder-audit assess`.
terms.why: It shows whether people could actually do what the stories promise, and where they would struggle, before you test with real users.

terms.means: A signal the app sends to its own analytics when a user starts, steps through, completes or abandons a journey; never user content.
terms.why: It shows how people really use the app, journey by journey, without ux-builder sending anything anywhere.

terms.means: What production data shows about a journey: completion, where people leave, failed searches, time per step (INS-<date>).
terms.why: It points to where real users struggle, which decides what to improve next.

terms.means: Showing a changed design to some users, measured against a success metric and guardrails, to test a hypothesis (EXP-1).
terms.why: A change is kept because it measurably helped, not because it seemed better.

ids.where: defined once in HELIX; the blueprint designs how the user meets it
the brief, and the design state
test sessions; the real name never leaves this machine

ids.kind: finding from a test or the assessment
observation by the design team (not user evidence)
